utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. You may be seated. Good morning, ladies and gentlemen; good morning to the technical booth. I think that everything is in order now. Good morning to the interpreters and the Prosecution and Defence counsel. We're going to take up the case where we left off. After this delay in starting, I have already asked the registrar, spoken to the registrar, for a memo explaining the reasons for which we started late. On behalf of the Trial Chamber, I should like to offer our excuses. I myself still am not aware of the actual reasons for which we had to start late, so I would like to have a written answer setting these reasons out by the registrar so that we can share these reasons together. We have certain preliminary decisions to make. I am turning to the Prosecution to ask them what their position is with respect to the protective measures requested by the Radic Defence counsel, and it is the request made on the 1st of March. Ms. Susan Somers, do you have any objections to the request made by the Defence? You told us that you were not in opposition with respect to the 19th and 21st of February. But now we have a third request, so may we hear your views on that, please. Ms. Susan Somers, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. If, in fact, the request is voice, facial, and pseudonym, the Prosecution has no objection at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. With respect to the 19th and 21st of February requests, and the one of the 1st of March as well with respect to the Mladjo Radic Defence, in view of the fact that the Defence team is asking the Trial Chamber to allow certain persons named in the request to testify and that they should be protected by a pseudonym, and in view of the fact that the Defence has also asked the Trial Chamber to grant protective measures with respect to facial distortion and voice distortion, and in view of the fact that there has been no objection by the Prosecution to that request, and in view of the fact that it is up to the Trial Chamber to ensure the security of witnesses giving evidence and fully respecting the principles of the public character of the hearings, and applying Articles 20, 21, and 22 of the Statute of the Tribunal and Rule 75 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, the Chamber accords the right to protective measures as requested in the requests mentioned. That is the ruling of the Chamber with respect to the protective measures asked for. There are other matters that we should give our consideration to, but we shall do that after the break. With respect to expert witnesses, we shall go into that matter after the break. We now have Mr. Fila, to whom I am going to give the floor for his opening statement. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I go ahead with my opening statement, I should like to ask you to bear in mind that the expert witness Ana Najman has been asked to stand at the disposal of the Court today because she is returning to Yugoslavia tomorrow. If possible, could she get through her testimony today. Your Honours, the accused Mladjo Radic stands before this Tribunal charged with crimes committed in the Investigative Centre of Omarska, in the period between the 24th of May, 1992 and the 30th of August, 1992. He is not alone but is one of a group of accused. So far we have heard the defence cases of Miroslav Kvocka and Milojica Kos. The Prosecution has tried to represent this trial as the trial of a policy of persecution and ethnic cleansing; as a person taking part in a well-organised and planned campaign towards the non-Serb population in the attempt to have the puppet regime of the Republic of Serbia turning its police forces and military forces against part of its own people in its search towards the great achievement of creating an ethnically pure Greater Serbia. I refer to the introductory statement by Mr. Niemann on page 6. In its opening statement, the Defence wishes to present its own standpoint in all the elements that are relevant to a determination of the possible criminal liability of the accused and by presenting its viewpoints in the following order: A, the historical context; the creation and disintegration of the Yugoslav state; the causes and development of the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina; the area of the municipality of Prijedor. B, the accused Mladjo Radic, his biography; the Investigation Centre of Omarska; an analysis of Article 1 of the Statute of the Tribunal; Articles 3 and 5 of the Statute of the Tribunal; accountability in the sense of Article 7 of the Statute, applicable law; the crime of rape; and finally, the conclusions. We begin with the historical context under A, the creation and disintegration of the Yugoslav state. The Yugoslav state was created after the First World War in 1918, with the unification of two then-independent states, the Kingdom of Serbia and the Kingdom of Montenegro, and the territory of the former Austro-Hungarian monarchy which is where the south Slav people lived; that is to say, the Serbs, the Croats, and the Slovenes. These territories, by decision of the National Council of the State of the Slovenes, Croats and Serbs, were conjoined to the new Yugoslav state which was called the Kingdom of the Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes at the beginning and later came to be known as the Kingdom of Yugoslavia. This state was a unitarian state based on the state thesis of one nation having three entities, the Serbs, the Croats, and the Slovenes. It was territorially divided into provinces known as the banovina which were not divided on an ethnical basis but on an administrative principle. In that state, the Serbs felt themselves to be nationally united. They were all living in one and the same state. So that they accepted the idea of a trinomial Yugoslav nation, consciously sacrificing their national and state individuality created throughout the nineteenth century. A decision of this kind was made by the Serbs already in the First World War when the government and the National Assembly of the Kingdom of Serbia opted for a joint state of the Yugoslav peoples. The thesis put forward by the Prosecution of a Yugoslav state as the realisation of the idea of a Greater Serbia has no foundation in historical fact. The first Yugoslav state brought to the Croatian and Slovenian people for the first time in their history a national and social emancipation for them. The offer made by the allies and voiced in 1915 in the London Agreement for the creation of a Greater Serbia was rejected by the Serbian government and opted for unification with the other south Slav peoples. Therefore the syntagma referred to as Greater Serbia for the first and only time was to appear then in international law and never again. The Kingdom of Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes, from its inception, was burdened by serious antagonisms. This was the result of the different and mutually exclusive state and national programmes of the Yugoslav peoples. Intolerance and latent separatism was expressed through the Croatian parliamentary boycott and forceful antipropaganda for the creation of a joint democratic united state. The Croats and Slovenes consciously abused the ideal of the Yugoslav idea. From the First World War, the Slovenes moved from the realm of the vanquished into the realm of the victors, and the Croats did the same after World War II. They moved into the realm of the victors and therefore sidestepped their responsibilities for wartime compensation and war damage claims. The representatives of Italy at the Congress of Versailles in 1919 for almost one year failed to agree with the beginning of the work of the commission for demarcation. It rejected to sit at the same negotiating table with the representatives of the vanquished powers because in the delegation of the new state of Yugoslavia, there was the representative of the Croats, Dr. Trumbic. The Croatian and political -- and Slovenian political elite looked upon the Yugoslav state as a period of transition in the process of state and national independence and autonomy. The Slovene, Anton Korosec, who was a minister in all the governments of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia from 1918 to 1941 explained the reasons for entering Yugoslavia, joining Yugoslavia, and this is what he said: "We have ridden a good horse and bled it dry." For the Serbs, the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes according to the ideals and idea of King Alexander I on the creation of the Yugoslav nation, which would emerge through barracks and schools, represented the age-long dream about a free life and a life together, of a unique Yugoslav nation, a united Yugoslav nation into a united Yugoslav state. In the 1930s, the Ustasha terrorist organisation was formed and its ultimate goal was the creation of an independent state of Croatia and the annihilation of the Serb population. The German invasion in 1941 represented the end of the first Yugoslavia and the beginning of the terrible suffering of the Serb people in the independent state of Croatia. Once the Ustasha powers established, an unprecedented persecution of the Serb population began, which turned into a genocide of the greatest magnitude. The Serbs were forced to defend themselves, to raise uprisings and organise resistance to the German and Ustasha fascist terror. With the allied victory in World War II, the Yugoslav state was formed once again, this time on a federal basis with six republics, Serbia, Croatia, Slovenia, Macedonia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, and Montenegro. As was differentiated from the other four republics, the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina were proclaimed republics with several constituent nations; the Republic of Croatia, as a state of the Croatian and Serbian people; the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was set up as a state of the Serb, Muslim, and Croatian people. The rule of the communists established in 1945 strongly suppressed national hatred, myths, and stereotypes, but the crimes from World War II remained unpunished. The victims and their executioners were reconciled under the slogan of brotherhood and unity, a universal formula for the solving of the national question of socialist Yugoslavia. Evil was encapsulated, shut up in Pandora's box. The leadership of the Communist Party of Yugoslavia, arbitrarily ignoring the political and ethnic realities, drew administrative borders between the republics, which several decades later became state borders. With the unresolved national question, those borders became the second major reason for the civil war. Chapter 2: The Causes and Development of the Conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Defence wishes to explain the genesis of the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina closer, and in that sense, the Defence has proposed the adoption of the expert report by Professor Nenad Kecmanovic. In the opening statement, I wish to stress the basic premises with respect to the general assertions contained in the amended indictment. From the sixteenth century right up until the Berlin Congress in 1878, Bosnia-Herzegovina was frequently the scene of battles between Turkey and Austria. The Ottoman Empire brutally stifled liberation movements and local rebellions. The local domestic Islamitised population was given the task of disciplining the rebels and their families which, for centuries, had fanned the flames and widened the divide between the converts to Islam and their neighbours. Hatred led to a reaction on the other side and this led to a vicious circle. The new occupiers who replaced themselves cyclically in these areas fanned the flames of hatred to a tremendous degree. By decision of the Berlin Congress in 1878, the state of affairs was sanctioned, in fact. And Turkey, after more than four centuries of occupation, was forced to finally withdraw from these parts. A system of relationships broke down which enabled many generations to have great privileges. Privileges were discontinued one by one, and the Bosnia-Herzegovina Muslims ascribed this disenfranchisement to the Serbs and their resistance to the Ottoman Empire. For their part, the Austro-Hungarian occupiers skillfully and systematically fanned the flames of intolerance amongst Serbs and the Muslims, as they did amongst the Croatians and Serbs so as to incite the already rebellious population. The repercussions were to follow in 1914, after the attempt made by Gavrilo Princip, who was of Serb nationality, on the life of Archduke Franz Ferdinand. This wave of violence against the Serb population and their property, which was taken spontaneously by the Croatian and Muslim neighbours, was to continue with the Austro-Hungarian declaration of war on Serbia and throughout the First World War. The fall of the Austro-Hungarian Empire in 1918, the breakthrough of Serb troops in the victorious march to the west, and the formation of a new state of the kingdom of Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes, under the leadership of the Serbian people, was viewed by the majority of local Muslims as being something far more difficult to bear than even the Austro-Hungarian occupation. This was the reason for the hatred of the disenfranchised beys and their attitude towards the new state and towards the Karadjordjevic dynasty, but also to their neighbours the Serbs as their old foes. The period between the First and Second World War, during that period, hatred festered. When, in 1941, we saw the breakdown of the occupation and command of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia and the formation of the Quisling NDH government, most of the Muslims experienced this as their liberation and welcomed manifestations of exhilaration in the hope that they might be given back their rights and feudal privileges. The Muslims en masse joined up to the Croatian patriotic army. Many of them put on Ustasha uniforms, so that together with the Croatian fascists, they should prepare themselves for a final settling of accounts with the Serb bastards, which, according to the Budak formula, would mean to convert a third, to expel a third, and to liquidate a third of the Serb population. With the end of the war and the reconstitution of Yugoslavia, Bosnia-Herzegovina was constituted as a federal unit. In the first postwar population census, which took place in 1948 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS

This is the subject -- what we are hearing is the subject of expert reports or testimony. This is not a road map to the case. The Prosecution strenuously objects to this type of information if it's only -- if this is -- certainly this is a judgement call on the part of the Defence, but this is not evidence. This is simply supposed to be used as an introductory overview to the case. As such, I think that it is an abuse to try to interject this much -- it is an abuse to try to interject this type of historical background without certainly giving the Prosecution to counter, because I think this is not, as I've indicated, the subject of an opening statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA

He mentions a Greater Serbia and the so-called Republika Srpska, and this is my response to Mr. Niemann's opening statement. So the opportunity that I have had to respond to Mr. Niemann, I shall give to Ms. Somers to respond to my own opening statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It took me a little time to hear the end of the interpretation. First of all, I would like to ask you all to speak more slowly. Ms. Susan Somers, what is your response? Have you had occasion to acquaint yourself with Mr. Niemann's opening statement? Can you give us your views?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have. In fact, the factual or historical references that are made are peculiar to this particular case, the facts of the case, and what is being presented to the Chamber, as I recognise it, is an historical overview which is properly within the realm of experts. I would not want to belabour it. I don't want to waste the Chamber's time, but I think it's important that this point be made. We strenuously object to this line. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fila, you may continue. If possible, you could abridge what you have to say perhaps; but if not, carry on as you have been doing. But please try and speak more slowly, and keep the interpreters in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the first postwar population census in 1948, 44.3 per cent, a confirmation was made of the majority Serb population. Subsequent population censuses showed that the structure was undergoing change. The Serb majority was slowly disappearing, and in the postwar period, the Serbs lost this numerical superiority. There were a number of changes, the colonisation of Vojvodina province being one of them, and the suffering of Serbs wherever war found them. Along with the changes in intensity, the Serbs felt that they were jeopardised, and migrations began when the federal constitution of 1974 was enacted. The republics were constituted by having all the prerogatives of a state, national ones, and republics constituted in this way cut across the Serb territorial and ethnic continuity. The time when the Republic of Yugoslavia, the SFRY, was defined, somewhat before the enactment of the constitution in 1974, the Muslim nation was constituted by members of this religious group. It is an incontestable historical fact that many Muslims, as members of a religious group, declared themselves and felt themselves as Serbs, to be Serbs, thanks to their recollections of their Serb origins and forebearers, which, at one point in time, under pressure from the Turkish occupier, had to convert to Islam. With the establishment of the Muslim nation, the Serbs who were Orthodox saw this as an intention to reduce the number of Serbs by an imposed political decision and not through the will of the Muslims themselves. At all events, those who, in the population census of 1944, declared themselves as Serb Muslims or Croat Muslims now became a new nation. They also suffered from the complex they had in the Second World War and the fact that they were termed a genocide nation by the procedures of the NDH. The NDH had its own way of dealing with the Serbs, to make them leave the territory where they had been until then. All these antagonisms in the postwar period had to be stopped, so that in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the sense of Tito's proclaimed policy, we should see the reign of brotherhood and unity in these parts. However, instead of the democratisation of relations, the powers and authorities resorted to recession, and all open national expression was seen as a crime and punishable by law. Religious customs and rites were looked upon in a negative form and as being a burden to anyone moving up the professional ladder in their careers. Unitarianism was not retained in the SFRY, and when the process of disintegration began, it necessarily expanded to the republics. The authorities tried to divide up public opinion, applying the system of divide and rule, divide et impera. Due to this, there was further distrust amongst the nations. Once characterised as nationalists and persecuted, the people began to turn towards their own matrix; that is to say, these Croatians turned towards Zagreb and the Serbs turned toward Belgrade. In the last period of peace, from 1945 to 1990, which is to say 55 years of peace, there were no conflicts amongst the three nations. And so the fact that they began to enter into conflict was ascribed to somebody from outside. However, that assumption is not correct. The process of the disintegration of SFRY began with Slovenia. The secession of Slovenia was accompanied with very few casualties but the casualties increased when the independence of Croatia was established and it got worse with the establishment of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Bosnia-Herzegovina experienced a tragedy because it was a nationally-mixed population under the long-term pressure of the communist powers, and this was different to Slovenia, which was an ethnically pure area. The pressure exerted by the communists in the period between 1945 and 1990 was a way of maintaining peace for these three -- amongst these three nations. In 1990, we saw all negative and destructive powers burgeoning, all of these protagonists having the feeling of being jeopardised. Emotions came to a head with respect to these nations' futures. Slovenia and Croatia said they would step down from Yugoslavia and the political leaders in the federal organ stressed that Bosnia-Herzegovina would not be anything more or anything less than the other republics. The Serbs, on the other hand, were realistically interested in maintaining and retaining Yugoslavia because their populations lived in all their parts and Bosnia-Herzegovina represented a constituent nation. In an atmosphere of this kind, and bearing in mind the fact that on the political arena of Bosnia-Herzegovina there was no democratic replacement to communism, the first multi-party elections were held. The results of the elections was that all the nations voted for their own nationalist parties. All three constituents nations in Bosnia-Herzegovina had their own visions of the future. The Serbs wanted to retain Yugoslavia. The Croats wanted Bosnia-Herzegovina to be conjoined with Croatia, and then to step down from the SFRY and to have the borders at the Drina River. The Muslims wanted Bosnia-Herzegovina to remain as it was, united and independent. The problem therefore lay in the fact that all three nations in Bosnia-Herzegovina were mixed up, so that it was impossible to have these enclaves form territorial wholes without moving the population. In Sarajevo, the organs of power and authority functioned in the form of the presidency, the parliament, and the government, composed exclusively of the representatives of the SDA, SDS and HDZ parties, which means the nationalist parties and their activities were of a purely technical nature. Important decisions were adopted -- it was very difficult to adopt decisions because there was majorisation by the two nations. And in the presidency, this was seen. In the government, in line with the electoral results, there were -- most of the ministers came from the SDA party and the decisions that were made were mostly decisions of the SDA party and Alija Izetbegovic. Fearing that the other two nations would realise their visions on the future of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Serbs within BH, wherever they represented a local majority, began to link themselves up in what was known as Serbian autonomous regions and not to follow the decisions reached in Sarajevo. The parliament in Bosnia-Herzegovina had one chamber, and it allowed for the possibility of majorisation, whether it was a constitutional substitute in the form of a council for the protection of internationality equality. At the request of 25 delegates, this proposal could have been outvoted and sent to that body for final definition. And at that assembly body, the decision was made by consensus. And so the proposal, which would be to the detriment of one nation, could have been stopped. In the night between the 14th and 15th of October, 1991, the Muslim delegation made the proposal that a decision be made on the proclamation of sovereignty for the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, to follow the example of Slovenia and Croatia. It was -- the Serbs were well aware of the SDA and HDZ's intentions, which was to secede, to have BH secede and separate from the Serb matrix. The delegates of the SDS party acted in line with their constitutional competencies, and 25 delegates of that party asked the request to be sent to the Council for International Equality. The Muslims and Croats failed to respond to that request and therefore drastically violated the constitution. In this way, all efforts made to solve relations in Bosnia-Herzegovina democratically fell through. And what was worse, the Serbs were told how decisions would be made in the future and the position they would find themselves in as a result. The Serbs therefore left parliament, and the most important decisions on the independence of any state was made in a half-filled hall without the participation of one nation. The Serbs went on to found a parallel parliament. They did not take part in the referendum on the sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina, whereas the Muslims and Croats did participate and in that way the conditions were fulfilled for international recognition which were established by the Badinter Commission. An indicator of further events in Bosnia-Herzegovina was an incident that occurred in Sarajevo at the time of the referendum, when, during a wedding ceremony near an orthodox religious building, the father of the groom was killed. This was a tragedy which led to reaction. The Serbs in parts of Sarajevo set up barricades and closed off portions of the town. The army prevented an escalation to this incident. Some mixed Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. military and police patrols were set up, but evil began to spread through Bosnia-Herzegovina: In Foca, Bijeljina, Bosanski Brod, and so on and so forth. An attempt to prevent a civil war, which was imminent, was seen in Lisbon on the 18th of March, 1992, when all three national leaders were ready to compromise, and they signed a compromise agreement. But upon returning to Yugoslavia, Alija Izetbegovic withdrew that compromise and the civil war was unleashed. The Area of the Prijedor Municipality. The area of the Prijedor municipality was known under the Turks as an area referred to as Knez Polje. The historical events in this area are practically identical to the rest of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. On the 31st of July and the 1st and 2nd of August of 1941 in the Prijedor municipality, the local Muslims and Croat Ustashas killed over 750 Serbs from Prijedor. Another 750 were captured during the night, taken to Prijedor, and liquidated once again. In Kozarac, there was a terrible execution of Serbs. Over 400 Serb peasants from Kozarac and Omarska were killed, and about 10.000 Serbs in the regions of Sanski Most, Bosanski Novi, Kljuc, Bosanska Krupa, Bosanska Petrovac, et cetera. In those periods of war, on the Prijedor territory, 5.000 Prijedor civilians were killed and 2.000 others lost their lives in the battles against the occupiers. In Prijedor, the Ustashas killed all the Jews as well. Since 1945, Tito's settling of accounts with nationalism, there was a peaceful period until the Croatian mass movement started. In that period, the Serb population in Prijedor worked as a component part of the state of Yugoslavia. Confirmation of this was that the last prime minister of the federal government, Ante Markovic, founded his party precisely at Kozara. At the meeting which was held on the 26th of July, 1990, 100.000 Krajina inhabitants rallied, most of them Serbs, and about 5.000 Prijedor Serbs, at the population census, declared themselves to be Yugoslavs. Prime Minister Ante Markovic, of course, was a Croat and the Serbs sided with him. Serious political confrontation on a national basis was the result because the local Serb population demanded that the cadres' organs be constituted on the basis of the realistic ethnic structure. That was fanning the flames of the fire because the Muslims and Croats joined forces, held meetings, flew their national flags with the chequerboard and crescent moon, and this reminded the Serbs of the mass personal sufferings during the war. Arms were procured from Croatia; people were arming themselves. The Muslims, where they lived, installed military polygons, camps, and so forth, dugouts. The elderly members of the Muslim families were leaving Prijedor, leaving just the young folk, the military-able men and the representatives of the SDA party. The representatives of [indiscernible], without the presence of the Serbs, decided on mobilising the TO, the malitia, and civil defence. Several days later, that is to say, on the 6th of April, 1992, the International Community recognised the sovereignty and independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The organs of power and authority in Prijedor, the Ministry of Internal Affairs of Muslim Bosnia-Herzegovina, sent an order to block and attack the military units. On the 29th of April, 1992, the Serb delegates in the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor took over power from the representatives of the SDA and Mayor Cehajic and prevented this order from being carried out. In the first days of May, armed members of the SDA and HDZ parties took over the Public Security Station of Ljubija and took the Serb policemen prisoner. In Kozarac, a military unit was formed numbering 3.500 Muslims. On the 19th of May, 1992, the Muslims blocked 10 kilometres of the Prijedor-Banja Luka road. On the 22nd of May, 1992, in the Muslim village of Hambarine, fire was opened from automatic weapons, attacking a military and police patrol, and two Serb soldiers were killed on the occasion during that ambush. In the town of Prijedor itself, in the early morning of the 24th or 25th of May, a strong group of armed Muslims, which had infiltrated the town the previous night, stormed the town with the aim of taking control. It received support from the numerous local population. In the street fighting, which went on for several hours, the rebels were destroyed and 16 Serb soldiers or, rather, policemen were killed. On the 25th of May, 1992, the Muslims attacked the JNA barracks in Prijedor, and on the 30th of May, 1992, they attacked the town of Prijedor itself. The way in which this attack was executed, it was obvious that it had been planned because it was precise and of a strong intensity, and there were many civilian casualties. A civil war broke out which was to have unforeseeable consequences on all three nations. This august Tribunal has been dealing, unfortunately, with these conflicts and individuals who found themselves in the midst of this conflict without their own volition. One of the accused was Mladjo Radic, and this period changed his life and he has become a victim. B. I should now like to talk about who Mladjo Radic is. I refer to his biography. Mladjo Radic was born in 1952, in the village of Lamovita, near Prijedor. Father, Rade and mother, Zorka. He had nine brothers and sisters. It is a patriarchal family, farmers who have respect for the customs and the traditions in the area where they live. The father of the accused Radic was a figure of authority for his family. The members of the family were and remain closely knit together by their belonging to the area, the customs, and the family. The accused Radic finished elementary school, and after school, as a child of seven or eight years, he worked in other families. The material means of his parents were very modest. That is why he only graduated from the elementary school and could not go on to further his education. He worked as a manual labourer and, after completing a six-month course, found a job as a policeman on the 1st of December, 1972. He was a simple policeman in Ljubija. Beginning with the 17th of June, 1992, he was again a regular policeman, the lowest level possible in the Police Station Department of Omarska. In 1993, he was assigned to the same duties in Prijedor, in the Police Station Prijedor 2. On the 1st of September, 1994, he was assigned to the job of shift leader in the Police Station Department of Omarska at the Public Security Centre of Prijedor. On the 20th of October, 1995, he was given the rank of sergeant first class. On the 1st of November, 1996, his employment was consensually terminated. In his 24 years of service as a regular policeman, Mladjo Radic worked as a foot policeman and was in charge of maintaining law and order in the street, securing buildings and people, and controlling traffic. In all his years of service, Mladjo Radic never once applied force in resolving conflicts. While working as a policeman, Mladjo Radic made his rounds and met a great number of people of all ethnic groups, and with many of them became friends. He visited them on religious holidays. He became close to some of them and became a godfather to some. It is important to note that in the area where he lived and worked, it was rare for such relationships to be established between members of different ethnic groups. Mladjo Radic is married and father of three. His eldest son, Drazenko, works in the police and is now the only member of the family making a livelihood. The relations in the family of the accused Radic follow the same model of the family in which he grew up; that is, they are patriarchal, and the only difference is in the changed image of the wife who does not conform to the patriarchal model. The relations in the family are marked by mutual trust, understanding, and respect. Mladjo Radic is to his sons a figure of authority whom they respect in every way. The events in Prijedor, the takeover by Serbs and the establishment of the Investigative Centre of Omarska, found Mladjo Radic as a policeman working in the Police Station Department of Omarska. He was told that the investigative centre was established for purposes of investigations and his duties would practically be the same as before, the only difference being that he was being assigned to the newly established investigations centre. His job was to secure buildings and people. In the given situation, he did not look for answers to questions regarding reasons for the existence of the investigations centre, nor did he display any curiosity regarding the work and functioning of the investigative centre. He simply took his duties as part of his job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, I repeat the same apologies to both the Chamber and to my learned counsel opposite. However, what is happening is the expert reports, or significant portions thereof, are simply being read to the Chamber under the rubric of opening statement, and I must object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Somers. Of course, the relevance of what the counsel has just said can't be denied. utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He accepted his assignment at the Investigative Centre of Omarska and his obligation to work as security and to provide guards as something which was ordered him by his superiors, in view of the existing hierarchy and subordination in the police. The Investigative Centre of Omarska was established based on the order of the Chief of the Public Security Station in Prijedor, dated the 31st of May, 1992. A document dated the 31st of May, 1992, that is, the order of the Chief of the Public Security Station in Prijedor, points out the real nature of the role which the accused could have had in the events in Prijedor and the environs in mid-1992. The document, which is evidence before this trial, shows who ordered the establishment of the centre, why, and what kind of organisation existed there. In other words, Omarska was designated as a temporary collection centre for persons who were captured in fighting or detained based on operative information at the disposal of security services. The totality of the work and the selection of detained persons is continued by a mixed group of investigators of national, public, and military security, point 3, and the persons in charge of these duties are named one by one. In point 4 of this document, the obligation of round-the-clock engagement of these persons is specified, with continuous presence of investigators in the collection centre. In item 5 of the same document, the further fate of the detained persons is clearly specified and it is exclusively linked to investigators as described in items 4 and 5 of the document. The line of command is established in the provision of item 11, which prescribes the obligation of the coordinator of security services to submit as required on a daily basis reports on their work. The control of the execution of this order is envisaged and entrusted to specified persons in accordance with item 17 of the document. This document dated 31st of May, 1992 is very important for establishing the role of the accused Radic within the framework of the Omarska centre. Namely, item 6 of the document regulates the service of security of the collection centre and entrusts it to the Police Station Department of Omarska. That is, the order which establishes the centre makes a clear and absolutely obvious distinction between persons who organise, investigate, conduct selection, and to make a long story short, decide on the fate of detained persons, and police officers who received orders in their capacity of police officers of the Police Station Department of Omarska to secure the collection centre as part of their normal duties. Other obligations, rights, or duties did not feature in the document. They were not envisaged, nor did they exist in reality. Professional and authorised persons - that is investigators of public, national, and military security services - ran the collection centre, while police officers, in keeping with their job and their educational level, provided security without being able in any way to influence the essence of the centre. All arguments made by the Prosecution to qualify Mladjo Radic as a person of superior authority who, and I quote, "participated in the abuse of the detainees in detention camps located in the Prijedor municipality" are arbitrary, inaccurate, and illogical. To accuse a village policeman who just served as a guard in a collection centre for the ethnic cleansing of the region of Prijedor and to establish his role in the pursuit of Serbian state strategy on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina is groundless in every respect and borders on the absurd. The principles of fair trial and justice would not be satisfied and could be seriously compromised if the Prosecution continues to claim that Mladjo Radic is responsible only because he is available to the Tribunal. The Prosecution must not take the line of least resistance and abandon the prosecution of people who are really guilty while assigning responsibility to a man who was in Omarska, but only reluctantly and only out of fear for his family. Therefore, the document I have mentioned defines in no unclear terms the nature of the investigative centre which was established on the territory of the Omarska village. The same document indubitably points to the persons who ordered the establishment of that centre, formed and divided the duties in the centre, and also defines the place and the role of the Police Station Department of Omarska and the police officers who were employed there. This document points to the changes -- the temporary character of the investigative centre, whose existence was only linked to investigations which continuously took place. After the end of the investigations, the investigation centre ceases to exist. That is why you should look at the definition, the definition of a concentration camp, and why it is inappropriate to call Omarska a concentration camp. However, this document goes a step further. It clarifies also who is not guilty, pointing precisely to the persons who really had authority within the framework of the investigation centre. It also clarifies the role of the accused Radic and it says clearly that his role is only to provide security. It clarifies therefore that what we have here is a manipulation aimed at painting Keraterm, Omarska, and Trnopolje as death camps the likes of Auschwitz, Majdanek or Treblinka. Article 1 of the Statute of the Tribunal. The Defence of Mladjo Radic, in its motion on the form of the indictment, indicated and explained in detail why it believed there were no reasons to try the accused as a person guilty of grave violations of international humanitarian law for the purposes of Article 1 of the Statute of the International Criminal Tribunal. I will not repeat them here. As regards Articles 3 and 5 of the Statute, the Defence believes that no serious objections can be made to the arguments presented by the Prosecution when explaining the possible application of Articles 3 and 5 of the Statute of the Tribunal primarily in light of the decision of the Appeals Chamber in the Tadic case, that is the decision on interlocutory appeal, as well as the position of this Chamber expressed in the decision on the motion on the form of the indictment dated 12th April, 1999. The Defence wishes to stress on this occasion as well that it does not agree with the arguments presented in the said decisions but it understands the principle of stare decisis and, in that sense, considers that there is no reason for further discussion. From the evidence presented against the accused Mladjo Radic, we can see that one of the principal conditions for applying Article 5 of the Statute is the grave, systematic, and widespread nature of the act. And that has not been met. A separate question is the question of the armed conflict on the territory of the Prijedor municipality in the period relevant to the indictment. It is not unimportant that the armed conflict lasted only two days, and at the time which is relevant to the indictment, it has been over for quite a while. This claim removes any grounds for the application of Article 3 of the Statute. The Defence of the accused Radic does not contest the legal premises which the Prosecution established for the application of this article based on the previous practice of this Tribunal. It simply points out that in this specific case, there are no facts which would justify the application of this right as established. Responsibility under Article 7 of the Statute. In this trial so far, we have heard various claims regarding Mladjo Radic aimed at presenting the accused Radic as a person responsible for the events in Prijedor and primarily in the Omarska camp in the summer of 1992. In its Pre-Trial briefs and in the opening statement of the Prosecutor, Niemann, the Prosecution has elaborated on this in detail. The Defence will now deal with the theory of command responsibility under Article 7(3) of the Statute. The Defence of the accused Radic believes that we can only speak of command responsibility if the following elements were to be proved: 1, the status of the accused as commander or as civilian who violated international humanitarian law and had power consistent with military or, in this case, police command; 2, that there has indeed been a violation of the international humanitarian law; 3, that the accused was indeed a commander or knew of committed violations of international humanitarian law or that he had information from which he could conclude, could have concluded that this law had been violated; 4, that in his capacity of a superior, he omitted to undertake reasonable measures to control violations of international humanitarian law by investigating complaints, punishing perpetrators, or taking steps to prevent further violations; and 5, that omissions of the commander, that is a person possessing the prerogatives of a commander, was the cause of a grave violation of international humanitarian law which indeed took place. The Defence further emphasises that the command position is a necessary prerequisite for imposing command responsibility. The Defence stresses that a factor which affects this type of command responsibility is primarily actual power and control in the behaviour in the acts of the accused -- of the underlings, sorry. The said commander cannot be deemed personally responsible for failing to prevent the execution of an illegal order carried out by his subordinates unless the conditions I have mentioned had been satisfied. These conditions, which I have read out, are set out cumulatively and, in the case of the accused Radic, have not been met, have not been fulfilled. The accused Mladjo Radic had no function at all in the Investigative Centre of Omarska, either de facto or de jure. The charges of the Prosecutor from the opening statement on page 64 to the effect that the accused Radic exerted power in the Omarska camp are groundless in every respect. The Defence has already presented evidence through the testimony of the accused Radic that Radic was appointed shift leader within the Police Station Department of Omarska only in 1994. One cannot accept the claim that Radic had already been shift leader because why would a decision then - and that decision is already on file - make him -- appoint him to that duty again? Meakic, as a commander, had no authority to appoint, discharge, or promote anyone, the accused Radic included. The investigation centre in question was controlled by the -- at the time by Simo Drljaca and people from the Crisis Staff. The Defence will prove that we cannot speak of him being a de facto shift commander either. Mladjo Radic was a guard, a police officer who served his entire years of service in village police stations in Ljubija and Omarska. It seems natural and normal to the Defence that commander Meakic, when the organisation of security of the investigation centre required it, ordered the accused Radic to also serve as officer on duty in the room on the first floor of the administrative building and to handle communication by telephone and by radio during his shift, which is one of the duties of a regular policeman. This fact, which the Defence claims to have been sporadic and exceptional and which could have appeared to detained persons as some superior function to that of a simple guard, and which the Prosecution wishes to present as a command function, entailing command responsibility under Article 7(3), this function of the officer on duty is in fact a logical situation because, among the guards which provided security, the accused Radic was the eldest in terms of his age. He was the only professional policeman on that shift, and he was the only one who could operate a radio and telephone equipment in the station where he worked. The Defence has already referred several times to the document by which Simo Drljaca established the investigations centre, which was signed by him, and we will do so now again, pointing out the fact that this document indicates all structures involved in the work of the centre. The army secured a broader area around the centre in a circle of a couple of kilometres. There were, and they are noteworthy ^, members of special units from the area of Banja Luka, about whom one report of Simo Drljaca himself says that they were out of control, that they beat and stole from people. At the entrance to the mine, there was the regular security of the mine. Within the security service of the camp, there were 19 soldiers attached to the security which were not under the command of Meakic. They had their own separate command. Only in the end can we talk about the policemen from the Police Station Department of Omarska with a great number of attached reservists. These reservists are people whom active-duty policemen do not know, as a rule. They ignore police procedures, and they joined the reserve force of the police usually to avoid going to the front. Their behaviour was marked by wilfulness, lack of discipline, and lack of responsibility for their own acts. The chaos of war in that summer of 1992 engulfed the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina and therefore encompassed the region of Prijedor municipality, and a state of anarchy, lawlessness, and arbitrariness of all kinds was projected on the situation in the investigations centre as well. The lines of subordination or chain of command had not been established. A firm command structure in the civilian and military segment did not exist. A higher structure of command contributed to the state of chaos and anarchy. You have heard that there were many victims and all of them said that everybody acted as they pleased, that nobody was responsible for their actions to anybody, and that there was general chaos. The situation in the Investigations Centre of Omarska was an expression of the anarchy that swept over Bosnia-Herzegovina. Mladjo Radic quite simply turned up to work one day and was given the order of going to the investigations centre instead of going about his regular duties. He was told that in Omarska, as an active policeman, he would serve for only several days, temporarily assigned to Omarska, and that afterwards he would return to his regular duties as a policeman. This temporary character and the anarchy that reigned throughout is an explanation of why a structure was never established within the centre itself, a firm structure, and why deputies and heads of shifts were not assigned despite the burgeoning work; but that the organisation was taken over as had existed in the police department. During the existence of the Investigations Centre of Omarska, Radic kept saying that it was temporary and that he would -- Meakic told Radic that it was temporary and that he would go back to his own work post. The Defence will show that Mladjo Radic was an ordinary guard to whom, from time to time, Commander Meakic assigned shift duty. The Trial Chamber has already had occasion to see on the television tape, to see the accused Radic at his guard post in the oval glass section of the administrative building, with a rifle over his shoulder. If you remember, in his opening statement, Prosecutor Niemann, on pages 23 and 24, said that there were interrogators/inspectors in the centre from Prijedor and Banja Luka, as well as the military investigation organs. They decided on the fate of the detainees, and it is upon their orders that they were sent to the various premises and investigated. The Defence will show beyond reasonable doubt that Mladjo Radic had nothing to do with any of this because he was in the centre as an ordinary policeman, a village policeman, reluctantly, against his own will, and temporarily assigned there. Throughout the duration of the war, as well as the Omarska camp, Mladjo Radic remained what he had been before the war, an ordinary patrol policeman on the beat. The Defence wishes to stress at this point that the Prosecution has not offered even two witnesses who would give identical and consistent testimony to confirmation of the fact that the accused Radic did anything that could be punishable by law within the frameworks of his work in the investigations centre. The Defence will show that Mladjo Radic, in fact, saved more than 35 people, at least 30 of them from Ljubija, and that through his own authority -- and that he did so on the basis of his own authority, because he was not able to issue orders to anybody. When we speak about the authority of Mladjo Radic, this can only be the authority of a good man, a man who has had a lot of experience and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. who is respected by one and all. In the opening statement, on page 17, the Prosecutor accuses Radic of being responsible for the conditions that prevailed in the investigations centre. Mr. Niemann states that the water that the detainees received was not pure and that many of them fell ill as a result of drinking it. The Defence will show that as regards accommodation, food, water, that Mladjo Radic had nothing to do with any of this. He was not able to influence the situation in which the detainees found themselves. The only thing that he could do and that he did do was to bring food, personal hygiene items, a letter or money to some of the detainees secretly, without anybody else knowing. As I say, he brought food when he could and as much as he could. He jeopardised the safety of his own family and his own personal safety in doing so. The water that was drunk by the detainees was water from the waterworks system, and it was the same water that was used by everybody. The same water was used before the war, during the war, and is used to the present day, that same water. He was not able to decide on whether detainees would receive visits or not; that was not up to him. The entrance gate was several kilometres away from the detention area. Finally, it is important to mention that many times during this trial we have heard people say that Krkan's shift was the worst. What does that mean? Did the Prosecution offer any witness who said that Mladjo Radic ever hit anybody or ordered beatings of any kind? Did Mladjo Radic kill anybody or order the killing of anybody, or was he even present while a killing took place? When the Prosecution witnesses refer to Krkan's shift, the witnesses say this because they know Krkan. And even if his shift was the worst, then there were only three men, three guards. Paspalj, Predojevic, and Popovic, those were the only perpetrators. But the composition of the shifts was determined on the first day by Meakic, and that is how it remained until the end. Let me repeat: The Prosecutor in this case has not even brought two witnesses, at least two witnesses who would describe the same event in the same way when it comes to Mladjo Radic. Finally, I am going to speak of applicable law. The Defence wishes to present its views on the legal character of command responsibility. For military or police commanders or other persons in superior authority to be considered criminally responsible, it is necessary for a norm of international customary law to exist prescribing that type of responsibility. The Defence wishes to emphasise that at the time relevant to the indictment, command responsibility as a form of criminal responsibility did not exist. After trials for crimes committed in the Second World War, not a single court at any time in the future has applied the rule of command responsibility as a form of criminal responsibility, nor has a single state introduced this rule in their criminal law. Many theoreticians claim that the rule of international customary law, which not a single state observes or enforces for a prolonged period of time, ceases to apply as a rule of international customary law. In Article 38 of the statute of the International Court of Justice, international customary law is defined as general practice accepted as the law. This means that this practice has to be general and continuous. The fact that after the Nuremberg and Tokyo trials, states have not made a single act which would manifest their observation of enforcement of international customary law on command responsibility as a form of criminal responsibility. In the meantime, a great number of armed conflicts have happened involving a myriad of horrible war crimes, and not a single court has applied the rule of command responsibility as a form of criminal responsibility. The practice of the International Criminal Tribunal in the cases of Delalic, Blaskic, and others quotes the Military Field Manual on Military Law of the United States and the British manual of military law as evidence of existence of command responsibility as criminal responsibility in the form of a rule of international customary law. However, the said military regulations -- however, all these military regulations prove is that states have accepted command responsibility as an important legal instruction for the conducting of military armed operations. These regulations prove that states have not accepted this institution as part of their criminal law, because if that were so, it would appear in their criminal laws. And that is not so, especially not in Yugoslavia. The Defence emphasises that Captain Ernest Medina was not tried for the massacre in My Lai committed in Vietnam by the United States, committed specifically by his subordinates, based on the rule of command responsibility contained in the Military Field Manual on Military Law of the United States, but he was tried on the basis of the uniform code of military justice which does not incorporate the rule of command responsibility. The same is true of Articles 86 and 87 of Protocol I to the Geneva Conventions of 1949. These legal rules, even after the ratification of these protocols, do not in themselves become norms of criminal law which could as such be applied to a judicial or disciplinary proceeding. Let us be clear. The norms of this protocol are elaborated in an operative way in manuals on the conduct of military armed operations, that is, in the form of military disciplinary responsibility. They do not appear in criminal laws as a form of criminal responsibility. I am saying this because I want to show the variety of interpretations in legal theory concerning command responsibility; whereas Mladjo Radic, a simple policeman, was expected, back in 1992, during his two and a half months of guard service, which was actually done only one day out of three, to know these norms of international humanitarian law and to follow them. The last part of my opening statement has to do with mens rea. The Defence wishes to also deal with the existence of mens rea as required by Article 7(3) which says "knew or had reason to know." The Defence emphasis that Article 7(3), with its formulation "knew or had reason to know," provides an ambiguous and unclear standard for mens rea which is not known from the criterion contained in Article 86 of Additional Protocol I, which stresses that the commander had to actually possess information based on which he could conclude that his subordinates committed violations of military law. The standards set by the Additional Protocol seems to be more acceptable to the Defence. Therefore, the Defence suggests that Article 7(3) be interpreted in such a way that a commander is deemed to have reason to know only when he actually has information enabling him to conclude that a violation of international customary law had taken place. In addition, the Defence believes that an evaluation must be made of the type and volume of information which a person, acting as a superior, may acquire in order to establish whether he had information enabling him to conclude that war crimes were committed. He must -- the Defence believes that it must be proved that the commander instigated criminal behaviour on the part of his underlings by failing to expose them and to intervene. Such knowledge cannot be presumed in the absence of direct evidence that the commander knew of his subordinates' crimes. The Defence asserts that we can speak of responsibility only when the person concerned took active part in the planning, instigation, ordering, aiding or any other form of participation in the execution. Regarding the accused Radic, the Defence claims that the physical membership in a police unit in itself does not prove that a crime has been committed. We can speak of guilt only if the condition has been met of the existence of intent, including awareness of the act of participation, together with a conscious decision to take part in the act by planning, instigating, ordering, or otherwise aiding or participating in the execution of a crime -- in the commission of a crime. In addition, the Defence stresses that the Prosecutor omitted to prove -- failed to prove any behaviour on the part of the accused which contributed to the commission of a crime. The Defence believes that in order to establish criminal responsibility on the part of the accused, in the sense of Article 7(1), it would be necessary to prove that the accused had specific intent to commit an act which would facilitate the commission of a crime and to prove the causal link between the action taken and the crime committed. Not a single piece of evidence presented by the Prosecution against the accused Radic has the Prosecution succeeded in meeting the necessary legal and theoretical standards which could be sufficient for finding the accused guilty on any charge of the indictment.
