utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: I was before this International Tribunal, I think, in 1998 - I apologise if I haven't given the exact date - and it was linked to the Dokmanovic trial. They were comments on the expert findings and I sat before this Tribunal, I handed in my written findings, and answered questions put to me. I think that it was in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What ethnicity was Mr. Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Well, I think he was a Serb, although I don't really know, to be quite frank. That was not important, but I think he was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Are you presently being retained -- your services being utilised by Defence counsel for another accused who is presently being prosecuted by this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Yes. Together with Professor Folnegovic-Schmaltz who comes from Croatia, I have spent the last three days testing Mr. Krnojelac in the Scheveningen prison and we completed that testing yesterday as regards the testing itself. We have not gone into our expert findings yet but we completed all that was possible in the space of time given us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you know the ethnicity of Mr. Krnojelac?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Through force of circumstance, yes, I do, because I think it was the day before yesterday that he told us. He said that he came from the surrounds of Foca, that he is a Serb, and we asked him some other particulars, so he went on to talk about his wife and in connection to this, Mrs. Folnegovic-Schmaltz and myself learnt of that particular fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Dr. Najman, have you ever been retained to evaluate Muslims or Croats who have been prosecuted by this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: The requests I received so far, I responded to them. There were no requests for any other cases so I was not called upon. I don't know about anybody from the Muslim or Croat ethnicity who was asked to be tested.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So can we take your answer as a no?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: That's right. I was not called upon to testify for any other persons, and to conduct an expert analysis and examination of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Dr. Najman, when you evaluated Mr. Radic in May of 2000, were you aware that if he is convicted of the charges alleged against him, he could be sentenced to a substantial term of imprisonment?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: I don't know. How I could know about that exactly, as to his conviction and prison sentence? I don't recall having discussed that with Mr. Radic at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Were you aware that if he -- if Mr. Radic is convicted, he could be sentenced to a term of imprisonment? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Of course. Of course I was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Would you agree, therefore, that Mr. Radic has an interest in the contents of the report that you produced?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: I don't know how you mean. Could you explain what you mean by that question? Have an interest? How do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, depending on what a professional like you writes in a report about Mladjo Radic, might affect a finding of guilt or innocence or might mitigate a sentence if guilt is eventually found. That's what I meant by an interest in the contents.

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: I did not gain the impression as a professional interviewing Mr. Radic that he was cooperating with us in any other way apart from doing his utmost to answer our questions and what we required of him, and I think that we wrote this down in our expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did Mladjo Radic bring any food or drink for you and your colleague when you commenced your examination of him?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: To be quite frank, that, as that was my first visit to the Scheveningen prison, that it seems to be a custom there, or perhaps a regulation. I don't wish to enter into assessment of what it was, but it was customary to offer a cup of coffee or a fruit juice or anything else, as he explained to us that he could procure in the canteen. And as the examination and testing lasted several hours each day, we were there for a long time and took a cup of coffee and I think a fruit juice on an occasion or something similar, but that was something that they -- that was accessible to them in the prison canteen, nothing more than that, if that's what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: My question was -- it's a very simple question: Did Mladjo Radic provide you -- bring you any food or drink when you did your examination? Is that a yes?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Yes. That was the -- well, not the food. It was just coffee and juice, no food. Coffee and fruit juice, no food at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for interrupting, Mr. Saxon, but what is the objective of those questions? Could you explain that to us, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The objective, Your Honour, is to show that this accused may have had an interest in the outcome of the report that this witness could have compiled, and was currying favour with the person who was making the evaluation of him. I'll move on, Your Honour. I don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead. We are here to understand as best as possible, so go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: During the course of your evaluation of Mr. Radic in May of 2000, were you made aware that Mr. Radic provided an extensive videotaped interview to members of the Office of the Prosecutor in March of 1999?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Would the contents of such an interview, statements that Mr. Radic made about the events in question of 1992, about which he is charged by this Tribunal, have been relevant? Would they have been relevant to your psychological evaluation of Mr. Radic?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Well, you've put me in a difficult position. First of all, I don't know the contents of that conversation so I don't know what the contents of the interview are, and you're now asking me to state my views as to whether that would influence the outcome of a psychological test on my part as an expert. So at this point in time, I don't know what to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. answer. I don't know. I'm not acquainted with the contents of the interview and yet you're asking me whether it would have an effect, whether it would be of influence or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You completed your report on the 17th of May, 2000, and by that date, several Prosecution witnesses had provided testimony in this trial. Prior to completing your report, did you review any of this witness testimony in order to see if any of those witnesses described Mladjo Radic and his conduct in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Is it possible that the contents of such testimony concerning Mr. Radic might have been relevant to your psychological evaluation of Mr. Radic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't know where all this is leading us. We just seem to be losing a great deal of time. Nobody, apart from this Honourable Trial Chamber, can allow the witness to look at a list with protected witnesses. That is the first point. Secondly, how can an expert witness state her views as to which statements would be of worth to her or not, the contents of which she does not know? She said she does not know about them; she has already answered that. So how, then, can she say whether something is valid or not if she doesn't know its contents? If the intention of the Prosecutor is to show the witness the collected works from this trial, I have nothing against it. We have five or six more years. I have three years until I retire. I'll wait, I'm happy to wait that time, if that is what is needed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The purpose of my question is simply to ascertain whether this witness used all of the information that was accessible to her at the time in performing the psychological evaluation of Mr. Radic, and the reason I asked this last question was because there was public testimony given by Prosecution witnesses prior to the 17th of May of last year. I simply wanted to know if she had an opportunity to review that or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fila, is there a problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, the transcript doesn't seem to be working, the English transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see that the LiveNote has not been functioning, that it ceased functioning after what Mr. Fila said. We have not received a recorded answer of what the Prosecutor said.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And another point, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us wait a moment, please. I think that the LiveNote is working again. Mr. Fila, did you wish to add anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By decision of this Trial Chamber, expert witness Ana Najman was requested to undertake an investigation, and there was a Dutch expert as well whom I haven't seen to the present day, nor do I know whether he had something to drink and eat in the Detention Centre. But that's not why I'm saying it. We can see from these assignments what Ana Najman, as an expert witness, and the gentleman from Holland were able to see. And it did not state that it was their duty to read the transcripts from this trial. That is the point I wish to make. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are now entering into the realm of allegations. I think that what Mr. Saxon is saying supposes a schematic of expertise. So before going ahead with your questions, ask the expert witness what the framework of the assignment given to her was, what duty and assignment did the expert witness have to carry out, without going into a discussion of what model it was. I think that the best thing would be to go directly to the matter at heart. Ask the witness direct questions and afterwards we shall be able to see where we stand. Mr. Saxon, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What were you asked to do, Dr. Najman, with respect to Mladjo Radic?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Dr. van den Bussche, who was the designated forensic psychiatrist, together with me for this expertise, we jointly received three questions to which we were to give together our opinion and answers. The first question had to do with the past and present intellectual and mental state of the accused Mr. Radic. The second question concerned the provision of all the relevant information for evaluating the mental state of the accused in connection with the crimes allegedly committed. The third task was to provide information on the present state of the accused and his potential for rehabilitation and reintegration, and any psychiatric or psychological recommendation that we could give. After completion of this psychiatric and psychological examination and psychodiagnostic tests, and after summing up the results, Dr. van den Bussche and I drafted our joint answers to the questions posed by the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You mentioned the second question concerning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, but there is again a problem with the transcript. Registrar, is there a problem or not?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, there seems to be a problem, and I will have it sorted. THE COURT REPORTER: It seems to be working now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Testing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I think we are now able to continue. Mr. Saxon, did you get the answer of the witness in the transcript? I hope you have. If it is in the transcript, you can carry on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I did receive it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You mentioned the second question or task concerned the provision of all the relevant evaluation for evaluating the mental state of the accused in connection with the crimes allegedly committed. My question for you is: Might it have been relevant to your examination if you had reviewed available public testimony regarding the conduct of Mr. Radic in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Well, I must repeat to you again what I have already said: I cannot declare anything in this respect because I'm not familiar with the content of this public testimony, and I cannot say whether it could affect positively or negatively my psychiatrist's impression of the accused Mr. Radic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The transcript, as I'm looking at it, quotes you as saying, "my psychiatrist's impression." Did you actually say "psychiatrist" or "psychologist"?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Psychological. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So was the only source of information that you used regarding the mental state of Mr. Radic, in connection with the crimes allegedly committed, the information that Mr. Radic gave to you himself during the interview?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'd like to talk to you a bit about the report that you produced.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe the Registry has copies of this report. I misspoke; I'm wrong. The Registry is about to receive copies of this report which could be marked as -- if it could be marked only for identification as Prosecution Exhibit 3/214.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you bring a copy of your report with you, Dr. Najman? I have some questions to ask you about it.

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Perhaps if the usher could assist me by placing on the ELMO the copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Turn to page 2 of the report, which has the words "case history" in English at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: That is page 3 as marked here, if we understand each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ah, it may be different on your version. That's possible.

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Right. I'll bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The section of your report that's called "case history," pages 2 to 3, at least of the English version, contains information about Mr. Radic's childhood and his family life and his work history. Is it correct, then, to say that this information was provided to you by Mr. Radic?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Would you agree that it's possible that the version of Mr. Radic's life that Mr. Radic provided to you could have contained a certain amount of bias?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: I apologise, I cannot hear the translation. I'm sorry, the microphone wasn't working. In fact, the headphones weren't working for some of the time and I didn't hear all of your sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you now. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'll repeat the question. Would you agree that it's possible that the version of Mr. Radic's life that Mr. Radic provided to you could have contained a certain amount of bias?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: The anamnestic version given by every subject that I examine as a forensic expert, and that I have examined for the past 15 years, is always biased. During my examination, I never look for personal documents, certificates of birth, diplomas, or any other certificates, nor does any other expert do it, because our professional ethics, the requirements of our occupation, require us to proceed that way. All the anamnestic information we get from the subject always come from the subject in his own words, and that is how it was with Mr. Radic as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What steps did you take to confirm the accuracy of the information that Mr. Radic gave to you?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: During our interview, we analyse what the subject has said and we always make a link, both by psychodiagnostic evaluation and thanks to the results of the tests conducted. I will now give you an example. For instance, if somebody says that somebody has a higher education, a university diploma, and during my examination and the interview I see that he has difficulty expressing his thoughts, that his vocabulary is very poor, that his handwriting is one of a man who is not used to writing and that he has difficulty completing tests, of course I will doubt his claim. That was just an example, which I used in order to try to illustrate to you how we proceed, how we professionally examine anything that the subject says.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You did not interview other members of Mr. Radic's family?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: No. I only interviewed Mr. Radic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And how can you be sure of the accuracy of the information that Mr. Radic gave to you and which you put into your report?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: I thought that my previous answer actually answered this question as well. However, I'll try again. The procedure in any forensic examination confirms what I have just explained. We do not require any documentation, we do not require any certificates. We accept anamnestic data as given to us by the subject. That is why the subtitle says from the anamnestist. The subtitle itself tells us that this is anamnestic information, information which originates from the subject himself. It's not data from a computer. It's anamnestic data, something that the subject says about himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Where in your report does it say that all information was provided by Mr. Radic?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Well, it probably doesn't say so in any particular sentence but the very fact that the title says from the anamnestist implies this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That word "anamnestist," where does that appear, Dr. Najman?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: In my report, on page 3, and I can see it here as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When you say you can see it here, can you see it in the English version?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: No. I see it in the Serbo-Croatian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'll move on. Let's take a look at the section entitled "Analysis of the Results for Intelligence Quotient Evaluation Tests."

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: That is page 4 in my text.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Actually, I'd like to go a bit slower. On page 3 of my version, there is a section entitled "Radic's Attitude Towards the War and Related Wartime Events." It's on page 3 of the English version at the bottom of the page. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: At the bottom of page 3 of the English version, under that heading, you write the following: "He was told that an investigation centre was being established for investigations, which would be conducted by others. His duty was to provide security for the centre. He did not inquire about its purpose or why it was set up, nor did he exhibit any curiosity about the investigations centre." There has been a lot of testimony given in this trial that a number of the former friends and colleagues of Mr. Radic were confined in the Omarska centre, or, if you will, the Omarska camp. Given that a number of Mr. Radic's friends and colleagues were detained at Omarska, did you find Mr. Radic's lack of curiosity a bit strange?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: His lack of curiosity, as I have already said a couple of minutes ago, did not appear to me to be strange, because his general global intellectual functioning is of the specific type. This implies a lack of curiosity or diminished curiosity, capacity for exploration, desire for finding explanations, and general inclination to exploration. To me, as a psychologist, this seemed to fit in the picture that he presented to me, and that was consistent also with the results of the tests. He is simply not a curious man.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Let's turn, then, to the section entitled "Analysis of the Results for Intelligence Quotient Evaluation Tests." That's how it's been translated into English. It's on page 4 of the English version of the report.

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Yes. It's on page 4 in my version too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Just waiting for the usher to be able to put it on the ELMO so that everyone can see. Thank you. At the beginning of this section of your report on page 4, you state that Mr. Radic's IQ is 90. To your knowledge, is there any margin of error to these measurements of IQ, intelligence quotient?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, you are asking me whether there is a possibility that I have made a mistake in measuring the intellectual capacities of this person. Is that what you meant?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm asking statistically, in your knowledge as a professional, is there a statistical margin of error to measurements of IQ, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Of course there is. Measuring intelligence is a very subtle job and a very difficult job for any practising psychologist. The result itself, in certain situations, depending on the state of the subject, the conditions of the examination, of the motivation of the subject to cooperate, it depends on all these factors. In the case of Mr. Radic, I had no difficulty with his cooperativeness. He cooperated to the maximum, as his capacities allowed him. We did not interrupt the process of testing, I mean this intelligence test; we did it all in one go. I was not able to determine that there could be other factors which could affect the results we got. I just stated here, if I can remember correctly, that there is an increased anxiety in him. I just mentioned it, but I didn't believe it mattered to the interpretation of results. In any case, that cannot significantly change the results. It's just the picture of the situation as it's developed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The statistical margin of error, would it be five points, more than five points, less than five points?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Less than five. Well, if you are looking for a precise figure, because we turn the results we get into the so-called weighed results, if there was an error in weighed terms, a mistake of five points would be equivalent to one or two weighed points.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Why didn't you explain that in your report?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: I simply did not deem it necessary. I didn't know that it could be important, and I could always mention it in my oral testimony. I could clarify anything if you ask me the specific question, and you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, I'm going to get to that in a minute. At the bottom of the same page, at least in the English page 4, you say the following about

utterances.speaker: MR. RADIC
utterances.text: "His current intellectual functioning is influenced to a certain extent by increased anxiety and a depressed sluggishness." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I see it. It's on page 5 in the Serbo-Croatian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How did you measure Mr. Radic's anxiety?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Anxiety is measured by clinical evaluation, and when I say "clinical evaluation," I mean it has to do with the experience of the doctor who is doing the examination. There is also a test which is a part of my expertise, that is, the Pluchick Emotions Index Test. It is mentioned in my report. Among other things, it contains a segment which relates to numerical expression of the existence or absence of anxiety. When I say "numerical," I mean that this is a measurable thing. It can be measured and expressed in numeric values.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Dr. Najman, how could you be sure that Mr. Radic's level of anxiety was, in fact, higher than it was before your evaluation?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: I have said that what we have here is an intermittent expression of communication anxiety. It says in my report, "a low level of education as a result of low stimulus in development and communications anxiety." I didn't see that this anxiety was high or low. I said it was intermittent, sporadic. As a forensic psychologist, it was my duty to write that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What you wrote, on page 4 of my version, was "His current intellectual functioning is influenced to a certain extent by increased anxiety." That was what you wrote. So I'm asking you, how could you be sure that Mr. Radic's anxiety level was lower prior to your evaluation?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I still haven't found this part. Oh, yes. Well, you see, this sentence relates -- in fact, it concerns the last part of the sentence. "His result on the verbal scale was 93, and on the non-verbal section of the scale, it was 90." Therefore, I reported that this difference between the verbal and non-verbal sections is partly a result of this increased anxiety and sluggishness, and I linked this with the result, which is 90, on the non-verbal section of the scale.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You said that Mr. Radic manifested a depressive sluggishness. How did you measure this sluggishness?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Depressive sluggishness is something that permeated -- in fact, I would rather call it subdepressive, subdepressive sluggishness -- that permeated our entire examination. Among other things, the Servexil B [phoen] scale measures it in the following way: The subject takes more time than the average person to complete some of the tasks. I measured the time, of course, because those are the rules of the test, of administering the test.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So are you saying now that Mr. Radic's sluggishness was not depressive, it was subdepressive?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Let me put it this way: They are nuances. They are very, very slight differences, refined differences, fine points which enable the investigator to make an assessment with respect to the course of the examination and testing itself. The psychomotor sluggishness or slowness in situations is always encountered when there is the quality of depression present.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You didn't mention these nuances or explain these nuances in your report, did you?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That's right, you did not explain these nuances?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Would you agree that the presence of anxiety and depression can make a person's measured IQ appear to be lower than it actually is?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So if --

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Generally speaking, of course, just as a general rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So if Mr. Radic was feeling anxious and depressed when you examined him, those psychological symptoms could have resulted in a lower IQ score?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: His level of depression and anxiety was not so marked or was not of a degree which would have an essential effect on the results of his test on an intellectual level. And I support this by the second test. It was Raven's Test of Progressive Matrixes and the results he obtained there were very similar. So that if this test was a test which was under the effects of this depression or anxiety, which might have been raised, then the results with Raven's test would give off -- would be quite different. I'm not sure if you have understood me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I've understood you completely, but if I'm confused I'm certainly confused at a higher level, so I'm going to ask you another question. Please try to help me understand something. You say that Mr. Radic's level of depression and anxiety was not so marked or was not of a degree which would have an essential effect on the results of his test on an intellectual level. Can you turn to your conclusion, please, which is on page 5 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can Mr. Usher please assist us by turning the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Dr. Najman, do you see the heading there that says "conclusion"?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In the second paragraph, this is what you wrote: "This somewhat increased anxiety, depressive mood, and general dissatisfaction with the situation in which he finds himself occasionally reduce his attention span and ability to concentrate and slow down his psychomotor reactions. All this together leads to the impression that his intellectual abilities are lower than his actual existing abilities." Isn't that different from what you've just told us?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: No. Let me explain. In this paragraph I wanted to say just one thing, and that is that Mr. Radic - and if we look at the last sentence, he is an individual with lower intellectual capabilities than they actually are as manifest, but in the first sentence I speak about primary intellectual potentials, because that was one of our tasks. Primary intellectual potentials represent potential which one has in life and with which a person functions, so it is not linked to the moment of measurement and they imply a certain capacity, which, put in simple terms, the capacities that we have when we enter the world, when we come into the world as human beings, and I assess that his primary intellectual potentials were also within the frameworks of this same particular category, and that when he was tested - and let us not forget that it was under conditions of detention, in a prison, and having spent many months in those conditions, in detention, that the communication and situation anxieties in detention was something that is to be expected, with practically all the detainees or any detainee.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, the situation in which Mr. Radic found himself in or was in when you spoke with him might have affected the impression that he gave to you and his responses during your examination? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: I don't think you understood me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Please explain, then.

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: What I said was that primary intellectual potentials are the potentials you're born with, you come into the world with. And now the measured intellectual potential is something that we measured at a given moment, and it is a fact or a number or category which we express via IQ units, units of IQ, and the moment in which this examination is conducted is something that we describe and it is our duty to describe this as professionals, and we say that it is accompanied by such and such a state or such and such a mood. And let me say here, if I may, that the process of testing the intellectual capabilities of a person is a highly refined task and a very difficult task for every examiner, and the subject, the person being questioned, notices this straight away and there is this malaise that appears very frequently. And I'm not only saying that in relation to Mr. Radic but generally when testing somebody's intellectual potential. It is a reaction that we come across very frequently because people don't like being -- having their intelligence tested. They don't like somebody seeing how clever they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In your conclusion concerning Mr. Radic's intelligence, on page 5 of your report, at least page 5 of the English version, you say: "Mladjo Radic's present intellectual abilities are at a level of normal, below average intelligence, that is one level below the average." On the previous page, at two places, you describe Mr. Radic's intelligence as in the category of below average intelligence within normal limits. Following your narrative report, you include copies of the results of a series of tests which you administered to Mr. Radic. The first test is called W-BI. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: On the first page of the test called W-BI, under the category diagnosis, you wrote, "Intellectual ability at the level of normal." Isn't this a very different diagnosis of Mr. Radic's intelligence level than you're putting in your narrative report? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: I assumed that you might have a question regarding this, and I did so for the following reasons. It is understandable that you should ask that because the scale of average, the lower level, begins with 91. The level of normal obtuseness ends with 90, normal obtuseness, and I think that you will understand this level of difference. The level of normal obtuseness goes -- ranges between 80 and 90. And the level, the lower level which we call lower level, begins with 91. In standard psychological terminology, this level of normal obtuseness is not expressed in that way. We say that that is intellectual ability below average. But in an official version of this kind, with a -- with binding categories related to psychology, I had to call this as it is termed, and the term is level of normal obtuseness, and there is no difference there. Perhaps there is a linguistic lack of coordination but what I say is level of normal obtuseness. But at any rate, it is a slightly lower level than the average. That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You don't explain this in your report, do you?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: I don't think that I explained it as explicitly as that, but on page 5, at the top of page 5, I did say that the level of category of normal obtuseness, 80, 90, is lower in respect to the average, which is 91, 110, and so on and so forth. I think that that is precisely what we have just been talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Let's talk about the section that's entitled "Description of Personality," if we can. And in the English version of the report, that begins in the middle of page 5.

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you see that heading?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: I can see the heading, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: On page 5 of the English version in the second paragraph from the bottom of the page, you describe Mr. Radic like this: "The subject appears to be an individual with reduced self-esteem, increased low spirits, a sense of hopelessness and frustration which is most probably a reflection of the situation in which he finds himself, and has depressive quality. In quality and level, this represents reactive depression. There is increased insecurity, anxiety, and distrust toward new situations and persons." If I understand what you're saying there correctly, you're saying in your report that Mr. Radic's condition of being incarcerated and prosecuted for very serious crimes affected, at least temporarily, his personality. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: I just want to ask you whether that is "The profile of Mladjo Radic has the following characteristics: This personality is characterised by the following traits," and then I go on to enumerate them. Is that what you have been talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: No. I'm actually referring to the paragraph above that.

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: "This personality is characterised by the following traits," that one?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: No, Dr. Najman. I'm referring to the paragraph above that paragraph, that begins with "The subject appears to be --"

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I found it. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Are you saying in that paragraph that Mr. Radic's condition of being incarcerated and prosecuted for very serious crimes affected, at least temporarily, his personality? Is that what you're saying there?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: I am saying that this depression that I noted during the tests and which I set out as the result of the MMPI test, I qualify it as reactive depression; that is to say, it does not have a psychotic quality and does not have the characteristic of a disease. It is not depression in the disease/sick sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Is it possible, then, if you examined Mr. Radic in 1997 prior to his arrest and detention, that Mr. Radic might have exhibited different personality traits than those characteristics which you saw and reported in May of 2000?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Radic, just like anybody else, would not have different character traits, because character traits are of a lasting nature, quality, in any individual; but their configuration, most probably, would take on a different aspect. So a different dimension would, most probably - and I say this only conditionally - would be more expressed. I am not sure whether then that depression would come first or whether it would only be slightly increased and marked. But in any event, characteristic traits and the ones I enumerate would have existed then too, because they are the lasting traits -- character traits are lasting traits of a personality, anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Let me use the vocabulary that you use. The configuration of Mr. Radic's character traits, isn't it also possible that if you had examined Mr. Radic in 1992 before he was formally accused of war crimes and crimes against humanity, that Mr. Radic might have exhibited a different configuration of his character traits than that configuration which you saw and reported in May 2000? Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is mistreatment of the witness. The witness has already said that character traits do not change. The configuration can be different but character traits do not change. If she has to answer that five or six more times, well, let's hear it seven or eight times more and then be done with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think that the witness saw herself to be mistreated, and I'm sure she'll answer the question. So continue. The witness is a psychologist so she is quite capable of answering the questions put to her. Please proceed, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Have you understood the question that I asked you, Dr. Najman?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I have understood the question, and let me repeat: Character traits are the lasting characteristics of an individual, but in certain situations, they are manifested in one way or another. They can be linked to certain external events, internal events, or feelings, and that is what a person expresses. In certain situations, they may be expressed differently. If somebody is a well-balanced individual, if they are emotionally stable, if they are in full mastery of their capacity and are able to strike a balance in every situation, for example, during the death of his parents or something, then a situation of this kind, whether it's death or anything similar, will result in a certain amount of depression due to the loss the individual has suffered. This will depend on a situation, but it has nothing to do with lasting characteristics, which we call character traits.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In the last paragraph on page 5, you say: "Mr. Radic's personality is characterised by the following traits: Loyalty, modesty passivity, servility, sensitivity, dependence, and a high degree of conformism." Aren't these personality traits which could be a consequence of being arrested and a prisoner in a strange country, or impressions which could be a consequence of being arrested and a prisoner in a strange country?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: I don't think the page numbers coincide once more.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It was the paragraph that you pointed out -- that you asked me about a few minutes ago, and I told you no, I was referring --

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I have it. I've found it, yes. "The subject appears to be," and so forth. "The profile obtained from Mladjo Radic has the following characteristics: This personality is characterised ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Aren't those personality characteristics or impressions, impressions or characteristics which could be a consequence of being arrested and a prisoner in a strange country?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Generally speaking, they could be. I discussed his results here, the results of the P test, the PIE, the Pluchick Index of Emotions, and the results I obtained I discuss in this report. Of course, it is certain that this feeling of depression that we have already talked about and the loss of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for interrupting, but Mr. Fila is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They seem to be discussing two different paragraphs, Your Honours, and that's where the problem lies. So I am just trying to be of assistance, if I may. Mr. Saxon is talking about the following paragraph, it begins: "This personality is characterised by the following traits: Loyalty, modesty, passivity ..." and you are talking about something else. You've gone up a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Saxon, I think this issue of communication crops up very often. When you deal with two different documents, you have that problem. You mentioned the page you have in your English version, whilst the witness has a B/C/S version. So make sure, please, that the witness is with you, is looking at the same paragraph. And please mind the time as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ms. Najman -- Dr. Najman, I'm sorry, the personality traits of Mr. Radic that you described in your report, anxiety, frustration, melancholy, indecisiveness, passivity, et cetera, could those personality traits be consistent with Mr. Radic's realisation of his actions in the past and the likely consequences of his prior conduct?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: In what sense do you mean "consistent with"? Consistent with his personality as it was previously, or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: No. I'm asking whether the fact that Mr. Radic may have felt anxious, frustrated, melancholy, indecisive, would those impressions or traits be consistent with a person with Mr. Radic's realisation of his prior conduct and the possible consequences of his prior conduct?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: As I said a moment ago, character traits are something which are the lasting characteristic and the lasting characteristic trait of every individual. In certain past events, we can carry out a reconstruction. That is very arbitrary, and I would not like to enter into the realm of arbitrariness at this particular moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, if I may enter into it, isn't it fair to say, Dr. Najman, that the entire concept of personality is a rather abstract concept?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: How do you mean abstract?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It's a subject that lends itself more to discussion and interpretation rather than precise measurement? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: I agree absolutely. You know, psychology is not atomic physics in any way and it never aspired to be. Neutrons have their nucleus and physicists know all about that, but - there is a great "but" - psychology has existed and has psychodiagnostic techniques which it resorts to and which it uses to measure certain characteristics of subjects, such as intellectual ability, character traits, and also what the subject himself does not wish to say about himself, something that belongs to his inner world. That, of course, is subject to discussion, can always be the subject of discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And the fact that these concepts and subjects are always subject to discussion, doesn't that make it very difficult to achieve scientific certainty with respect to the characteristics and changes of a person's personality?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Generally speaking, it is difficult, yes. However, a psychologist or a psychiatrist who is very close to -- and psychiatry is linked to our profession, and if you undertake the examination of a subject, in addition to psychological tests and discussions you have with the subject, and the assessments, psychodiagnostical ones, on the basis of all the knowledge that he has as an expert, and the field has, is able to arrive at certain conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In your section entitled --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Saxon, do you have any idea of the time you still have or do you want me to call your attention to it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: It was my understanding I had an hour and 15 minutes, and I understood that we began at 2.30 which means I would have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. You started at 2.20.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. May I ask one more question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. [English] Go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You mentioned in your report under the heading "Psychological Analysis and Interpretation" -- could you find that heading, please? Could the usher please help us again? You see that section, Dr. Najman?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: At the very last sentence of the first paragraph, you wrote regarding Mr. Radic: "He was not impulsive or aggressive in his life and professional career." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: I see that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Suppose hypothetically you were asked to evaluate the personality of a policeman; you received a report that one day this policeman and some of his colleagues were guarding prisoners as they came for a meal; according to this report, this policeman and his colleagues beat prisoners as they entered a restaurant area to take their meal; furthermore, according to the report, this policeman gave a sign to his colleagues for the beatings to begin. What observations would you make about the personality of that policeman?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Well, you see, our positions are obviously different. I am a forensic psychologist, and I distinguish between various types of aggression. Aggressiveness can be a potential of a person, a personality, and it usually belongs with disorders, personality disorders, and it's called psychopathy. Aggressiveness can be displayed occasionally. It can be shifted aggressiveness, and it does -- it is not necessarily a part of a personality. It can be displayed only in some situations. And that does not mean that the person in question has an aggressive potential within themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Were there two different methodologies used in the examination of Mr. Radic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I just ask one question? How many last questions does this Prosecution have? One, 2, 3, 23? Mr. Saxon said he only had one question. He is wasting my time mercilessly. I'm sorry, but I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Saxon?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise that I have gone overtime and I will withdraw the question and sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you finished. It is also for the purposes of the transcript, you know we mentioned 2.30, 2.20. We were wrong because if you had started at 2.20 or 2.30, you would have had half an hour left over. So that's clear. Often you require to be entitled to raise another question which encapsulates in itself another question, but here you moved on to another field of investigation or questioning so I think you have concluded the cross-examination. Mr. Fila, do you have any additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly, I'd like to find one thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The gentleman who did the expertise with you is a Dutch psychologist?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Does he examine Dutch people or other people?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Excuse me. This is going -- it's going too fast. Will you please ask counsel not to overlap?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Have there been any differences between you and the Dutch gentleman during your examination?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Diagnostically, there were no differences. As far as the approach to the subject is concerned, there were also no differences, and we had a very good professional cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Although you examined Serbs and he examines Dutch people?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And you had coffee and drinks together?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Judge Riad, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I think I can say good afternoon, doctor, now it's afternoon. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: -- profession which I didn't have the great advantage of being acquainted thoroughly with -- but just for my knowledge, you were just mentioning that you take in many elements in your examination and you include in it what the subject does not want to say about himself. I think you have another dimension. What about the subject giving you inaccurate information? How do you handle that?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: First of all, if the information is incorrect - I must say we always presume that anamnestic data is always correct, especially in situations when the subject is in a prison or under investigation. As far as other inaccurate information is concerned, if it concerns his personal traits, for instance, there are techniques to indicate this. One of these techniques is the MPI test which shows when somebody is lying, to put it simply, and there are other techniques such as the Rorschach test which gives a picture of the inner world of the subject which he does display in a way indirectly and which we are able to interpret. So these are very important indicators for us, and based on them we make our conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So you trust your indicators, that being in the hands of your patient, who perhaps can convey to you information which he thinks is right, is not lying?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: -- which is not at all the truth except in his mind?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: How do you handle this? I'm just wondering -- professionally, I mean, that's a problem. I don't expect you to answer it. And the other thing, you were just saying that aggressiveness can be displayed occasionally and not be inherent to the -- as I understand it -- to the real character of the person. In that case, then, in your analysis -- the end of the analysis, you cannot affirm that this person is not able to commit something. He can still do the thing even if the analysis does not lead to that, the conclusion does not lead to that. Is that a fair assessment?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: That would be one of the conclusions, but I must say that if a person does not have aggressive potential in the structure of his personality, then even his situational - if I can call it that - display of aggressiveness cannot be of a high level. It can be occasional rage or anger, dissatisfaction, but it cannot cross over into a level of aggression which is expected of a person who has aggressiveness within their personality structure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Riad. Judge Wald?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Doctor, I have two short questions. On page 6 of the English version, I'm just going to read two sentences and I don't have the Serbo-Croatian version so I can't tell you, but they come just above something called "Projective Material Results." Can you find where the topic heading is "Projective Material Results"? Okay. The two sentences just above say: "The dimensions of obedience, gullibility, dependence, and suggestibility are pronounced. Such a personality lacks a critical ability and independence as a result of which he constantly seeks support. In new situations, he demonstrates a greater degree of stereotypical behaviour and less flexibility." Now, on the following page - these will come together - on the following page, under "Psychological Analysis and Interpretation," in the third paragraph, you talk about Mr. Milgram and you say, describing an obedient person, that sometimes if he's carrying out acts under orders, you say, "in this way, ordinary people who are simply doing their jobs may become actors in a destructive process," and you go on to give the example of the soldier dropping the bomb. My question is the following: Taking the personality characteristics that were described in the first paragraph, not Mr. Radic, just such a personality, would you say that such a personality, when he or she is put into a new situation in which people around him are behaving very badly, very aggressively, in ways that normally this person would never behave in, that that personality is likely to begin to act that way too or not? Or to retreat or to object to the way that other people are acting? In a new situation that's quite new, as I say, when normally that person would not behave that way but he's in a situation where there are other people behaving that way, what would be the most predictable reaction? Not Mr. Radic, but of a person with these personality characteristics. That's my question.

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: I understood your question. The most predictable reaction would not go towards opposing, especially not opposing a group or people surrounding that person. I have referred here to Milgram's exploration of the subject because it mentions execution of orders which come from authorities. Many researchers have dealt with this, trying to clarify what you are interested in. The authority in this situation would have to be something -- someone who is seen by the subject as a figure of authority, either in terms of hierarchy, business relationships or family relationships. Also, since the order is coming from this figure of authority, it is this figure who is responsible for the act. The subject himself - I'm underlining this as a psychological interpretation, not a forensic or judicial one - the subject does not have the impression that he is responsible and that his own motivations and decisions have anything to do with it. This is the image that the subject has of his own act.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Just one short follow-up on that. Now, I understand your answer with regard to an authority figure giving an order. But the earlier quote talked about suggestibility and constantly seeking support. What if that person, that personality, doesn't have an order to do something but everybody around him, his colleagues, are behaving in a certain way that he would not normally behave, is it likely that he is going to, in order to curry their favour, behave that way or not?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: Well, what we lack here is initiative. Such a person does not have enough initiative to undertake something of their own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Wald. I have only one question for you because we could, of course, discuss this report for hours and days. Just this question: What was your training in this very specific field of forensic psychology, also called judicial psychology?

utterances.speaker: ANA NAJMAN
utterances.text: You mean my educational attainment? I graduated from the Faculty of Philosophy of Belgrade University, the group for psychology. I had three years of internship, specialist training, and I had also specialisation training. I worked in the prison hospital in Belgrade. I have been a forensic expert since 1985 or 1986. I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very good. I think we have put all the questions that we wanted to raise. Thank you very much for coming to the Tribunal, for cooperating with the Tribunal, and we wish you a very good journey back home. I shall ask the usher to accompany you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like -- Your Honour, I don't know whether Mr. Saxon wishes to tender into evidence the written report and the opinion of the forensic expert, Mrs. Ana Najman, or shall I do that? In any case, I believe it should be tendered into evidence. The Prosecution presented this so I'm not really clear on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had merely marked it for identification purposes. It is the report, obviously, of Mr. Radic so we will leave it to them to offer it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, we tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, what is the number for this exhibit?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number is 3/214 -- oh, I'm sorry, that's the Prosecutor's ID number. Just a second. It would be D30/4.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's what I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, what's the logic of it? What's the "4" for? What is it for? You said "/4." Why do we have "/4"?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Because the previous number was D30/3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're not going to waste any time on this right now. We've got the document; it was identified. We've Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. got to keep the same method of marking and identifying the documents. For the Defence, we've got documents that are identified according to the order in which the accused are stated in the indictment. That has to be taken into account. Anyway, we'll see about it tomorrow. You're going to have time in the meantime to think it over. Mr. Saxon, do you have any objection with regard to the tendering into evidence of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The Prosecution does object to the admission of this document, Your Honour, based on questions related to its reliability. The Prosecution does not believe that the findings or the conclusions of Dr. Najman's report are valid, and therefore we would object to its admission.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to make one clarification. Both reports constitute a joint report. Mrs. Najman examined Serb persons and the Dutch gentleman examined Dutch subjects. I don't know if Mr. Saxon objects to both Serb and Dutch subjects, or is it only one group that he has a problem with?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The Prosecution objects to the admission of Dr. Najman's report and the report that was presented by Dr. van den Bussche. So if we want to refer to them as one joint report, the Prosecution would object to the admission of both reports, or as a single joint report based on questions as to the reliability of the findings of these reports, how these examinations were performed, and the conclusions therein.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Three things. First, in the case of Mr. Kvocka, you admitted such a report. This Trial Chamber admitted this report. Second, that psychiatrist was designated by this Trial Chamber not myself. So I would like an understanding to be reached between the Trial Chamber and the Prosecutor's Office who is being accused of incompetence, I mean this gentleman from the Netherlands. The report is a single report. To cross-examine for an hour and a half and then say that the person is incompetent, I really don't see the point. I therefore insist that this document be admitted as a single report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Fila, but that's why the Trial Chamber is there, to make decisions. Madam Registrar, do we have a number now or are you thinking about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Saxon, we have to come to an end.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Just as a suggestion, it might be worthwhile, before making a final decision then, to allow the cross-examination of the other -- it might be possible, before the Trial Chamber rules on the admission of this joint report, to allow for the cross-examination of Dr. van den Bussche, who was the psychiatrist who examined Mr. Radic, and then a decision could be made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Saxon. Did you ask to cross-examine Dr. van den Bussche as well as Dr. Najman?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You know that we have problems with time, and I'm starting to have some doubts as to whether we'll be able to conclude at all. I know that the Trial Chamber issued the order for this expert witness. We've had the reports for a long time. We're trying to make headway but we are meeting with a lot of problems. We're not going to make a decision today. The Trial Chamber will ponder the matter. What we now have is a request for admission of the report. You have an objection by the Prosecutor. We are aware of your reasons. We're going to analyse the whole thing and make a decision, but we're going to leave it at that today, because we've been working for awhile. Tomorrow we'll be in court at 9.20. See you tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
